text: Chapter 4 follows one capstone — the earlier proposal's three-versus-five-qubit GHZ and zero-noise-extrapolation comparison — through building, running, analyzing, handling the unexpected, iterating, and finalizing. This lesson covers the build step: turning your proposal into working, testable code before you spend any real queue time on it.

This lesson covers why you build and validate on a simulator before ever submitting to real hardware, a concrete checklist for what 'built' actually means before you run anything for real, how to structure your code so a later unexpected result is diagnosable rather than a mystery, and a worked build plan for the running capstone example.

Every piece of your setup should run correctly on a noiseless local simulator before it ever touches real hardware. A noiseless run should produce the exact theoretically predicted GHZ measurement distribution, which gives you a hard, known-correct check on your circuit construction, completely independent of hardware noise. A bug in your circuit shows up immediately against this known target — it would be far harder to spot once real hardware noise is also in the picture, which is why this check matters more than the queue-time savings alone.

Before spending real queue time, confirm: the circuit construction produces the theoretically correct distribution on a noiseless simulator, verified not assumed; the noise-scaling and folding logic runs on a simulator with an injected, controlled noise model, with larger scaling factors showing visibly more degraded distributions; the Richardson extrapolation fitting code produces a reasonable-looking estimate, not one wildly extrapolating past your actual data range; and your data-recording format is decided and tested now, on simulator output, not improvised later under queue-time pressure.

The single biggest factor in whether a later unexpected result is a quick diagnosis or a frustrating mystery is whether you structured your code to isolate each stage: save the raw measurement counts from each shot batch, not just the final probability; save the per-scaling-factor results before extrapolation, not just the final extrapolated number; and log which device and calibration timestamp each real-hardware run used.

For the running capstone: build a function that constructs the GHZ circuit, tested against the known-correct distribution for three qubits; a function implementing unitary folding, tested against an injected-noise model where degradation should increase with the scaling factor; and a Richardson extrapolation function, tested on simulator-generated data where the true zero-noise answer is already known — so it can recover that known answer before you ever trust it on real hardware's actual unknown noise. Next lesson actually submits jobs to real hardware, in a way that produces a trustworthy, analyzable record.
